name: wrapper-facade
intent: Encapsulate a non-object-oriented API - C functions, raw syscalls or the byte-level routines of a wire protocol - behind one cohesive class (or handle type plus function cluster) that owns the underlying resource, coalesces calls that must happen in order, and presents a safe, portable interface to application code.
problem: The interface the application needs is a cohesive object with a lifetime, but the API it must call is a loose set of functions and raw data structures: a file descriptor plus open/read/write/close, a mutex variable plus init/lock/unlock/destroy, a device handle plus create/query/release, a protocol plus frame-encode/decode steps. Calling that API from everywhere scatters resource ownership, call ordering, error checking and platform differences across the codebase, so every new call site can leak a handle, skip a check or hard-code one operating system.
context: Systems software - portable daemons and services, device or FFI integrations, protocol implementations, libraries that must build on several platforms - where the boundary to the non-OO API is crossed from many call sites, where the underlying resources need deterministic release, and where the same application code has to run over different operating systems, library revisions or protocol versions. The facade is written once per cohesive abstraction (thread, mutex, socket, file, codec, protocol session) and becomes the portability layer the rest of the system is built on.
benefits: One concise, robust call surface: many low-level functions collapse into a few intent-named methods, so call ordering and error checking are written once instead of being re-derived at every call site.

Portability by construction: platform, library and protocol differences are isolated inside the facade's method bodies or per-platform implementations, while application code sees one uniform interface.
Deterministic ownership: acquiring in the constructor/open and releasing on teardown makes leaks, double closes and forgotten unlocks structural errors rather than call-site mistakes.
Type safety at the boundary: a typed handle replaces void*, a bare int descriptor or IntPtr plus errno, so the compiler rejects mixes the raw API would silently accept.
Structure upgrade: physical design entities (files full of #ifdefs, per-platform source sets) become logical ones (classes, implementations), which is easier to read, review and evolve.

A seam for the architecture above: dispatchers, connection handlers and lock strategies can be written against the facade, and a fake facade makes those layers testable without the operating system, the device or the network.
Incremental adoption: call sites migrate one at a time because the facade coexists with the raw API and can hand the native handle back for the cases it does not yet cover.
tradeoffs: A forwarding layer that must be kept in step with the wrapped API: new functions, flags and error codes keep arriving and the facade becomes their gatekeeper and change bottleneck.

The leaky-abstraction dilemma: expose too little of the raw API and callers cannot do their job; expose everything and the facade degenerates into a one-to-one rename that doubles the surface without adding cohesion.

Lowest-common-denominator semantics: capabilities that exist on only one platform or in one library version are dropped or hidden behind conditional extensions, so the uniform interface is weaker than the union of the raw ones.

A wrong wrapper is worse than no wrapper: ownership transfer, thread-safety of a shared native handle and error translation are contracts that, when wrong, hide the underlying call and make the fault harder to localise.
Cost of the indirection: direct forwarding is normally inlined away, but a virtualised facade (the Bridge-style variant) adds dispatch, can defeat inlining and complicates value semantics.
Debugging distance: native return codes, errno and stack frames get reworded unless the facade deliberately preserves the original code and context.
Duplicated effort when the wrapper already exists: hand-writing a facade over an API whose standard library already wraps it adds code, tests and update work for no gain.

participants.responsibility: One or more classes (in C: an opaque handle type plus its function cluster) that cluster a cohesive group of low-level functions into intent-named methods, own the underlying resource, coalesce calls that must be ordered, and forward each operation to the wrapped API.

The non-OO API being encapsulated - syscalls and their descriptors, pthread/Win32 synchronization calls and their handle variables, a C library's create/destroy functions and structs, a protocol's encode/decode routines - grouped by the abstraction they jointly implement.
Application code (and the layers above: dispatchers, handlers, strategies) that calls only facade methods and never the raw API, so the implementation behind the interface can change.

The platform-, library- or protocol-specific method bodies behind the uniform interface, chosen at compile time (#ifdef or per-platform source set) or at run time through dynamic dispatch - in which case the facade plays the Abstraction role of a Bridge.

use_cases: A portable daemon or service that must build on several operating systems: wrap the OS threading, synchronization and socket APIs once and keep everything above it platform-neutral.
Integrating a third-party C library (codec, database driver, device SDK) that hands out opaque handles and expects create/use/destroy ordering: wrap each handle in a type that owns it.
Implementing one side of a wire protocol: encapsulate framing, encoding and decoding behind a session object so application code sends messages instead of managing byte buffers and partial reads.

Giving the layers above a seam: define the facade as an interface and provide a fake or recording implementation so dispatchers, handlers and business logic can be tested without the OS, the network or the device.
Keeping a binary interface stable across library versions: publish an opaque-handle (pimpl-style) wrapper so the implementation can change without recompiling or breaking clients.
Encapsulating a legacy in-house C API (globals, callback tables, errno conventions) while new code is written in a higher-level style, migrating call sites incrementally.

ACE (Adaptive Communication Environment): the ACE_OS namespace and the C++ Wrapper Facade layer over it wrap POSIX, Win32 and RTOS calls - threads, locks, sockets, IPC, timers, memory - so the framework's higher layers (Reactor, Proactor, Acceptor-Connector) compile unchanged across dozens of operating systems from a single source tree.

.NET's System.Runtime.InteropServices.SafeHandle and the Microsoft.Win32.SafeHandles family (SafeFileHandle, SafeWaitHandle, SafeRegistryHandle, SafeProcessHandle): each derives a facade per OS handle type, overriding IsInvalid and ReleaseHandle so CloseHandle-style teardown, ownership (ownsHandle) and double-close protection live in the wrapper instead of every P/Invoke call site.

Rust's standard library as the canonical modern instance: per RFC 3128 (I/O Safety), std::fs::File, TcpStream and UdpSocket own a raw file descriptor and close it exactly once on Drop, while std::os::fd splits RawFd, BorrowedFd<'a> and OwnedFd so the wrapper's ownership contract is enforced by the type system rather than convention.
avoid_when: The API is already object-oriented and cohesive: use or adapt it (Adapter) instead of wrapping it again - a second layer adds cost without hiding anything.
The wrapper would be a mechanical rename of every function with the same flags and error codes and no coalescing, ownership or portability gain: depend on the API directly or generate the binding.
Only one or two functions are called, from a single place: an ordinary helper function is simpler than a type with a lifetime.
A maintained facade already exists for that API in your ecosystem (standard library, well-kept binding package): use it and spend the effort on the code above it.
The call sits in a hot inner loop where even a non-inlined forwarding call is measurable: measure first and keep the raw call on the critical path.
The API's natural shape is bulk or columnar (buffers, spans, batches): allocating a wrapper object per handle adds churn where a function over a buffer is the right interface.
anti_patterns: Mechanical rewrap: the facade mirrors the raw API one method per function with the same flag integers and error codes, so callers learn nothing and the API surface doubles.

Handle leak by design: the facade hands out the native handle or pointer as the primary way to work with the object, so callers close it twice, keep it past destruction, or manipulate state the facade assumed it controlled.
Objectifying everything: shredding a library's functions into dozens of tiny one-method classes until the cohesion the pattern exists for has disappeared.
Silent error swallowing: translating failures into best-effort returns or a log line, so the underlying problem is invisible at the call site that caused it.
Lowest-common-denominator plus untyped escape hatch: a uniform interface that hides platform capabilities and then re-exposes them through an undocumented native accessor.
Virtualising what never varies: making every method virtual for hypothetical extensibility, paying dispatch and inlining costs for an implementation that has exactly one form.
design_principles: Information hiding: the handles, flags and call ordering of the wrapped API never leave the facade.
Single responsibility per cluster: one facade per cohesive abstraction, with minimal coupling between facades.
Separation of concerns: platform-dependent mechanism lives inside the facade, application-level policy lives above it.
Dependency inversion: clients depend on the facade's interface, not on the foreign API, so implementations and fakes can be substituted.
Fail fast with ownership: establish the resource in the constructor/open, release it on teardown, and propagate the real error code instead of a neutral return.
best_practices: Cluster only functions that belong to one abstraction; when an API covers several, split it into several facades instead of one god class.
Coalesce calls that must happen in a fixed order into a single method, so init/lock/unlock/destroy ordering cannot be forgotten.
Name methods after the abstraction's intent, not after the wrapped functions: the facade's vocabulary should be the application's.
Own the resource: acquire in the constructor or factory, release in the destructor, close(), defer or scope-exit hook; delete copying and allow ownership transfer explicitly.
Forward inline and avoid virtual dispatch unless a second implementation really exists; add the indirection later, at the Bridge seam, when variation appears.
Convert errors at the boundary but keep the original code: throw or return a facade error type carrying the underlying errno/HRESULT/error name.
Isolate platform variation in one place - conditional method bodies or per-platform implementation files - and keep the published interface platform-independent.
Keep a documented escape hatch (native_handle(), as_raw_fd()) for what the facade does not yet express, and review every use of it.
sources: Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert & Buschmann, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture, Volume 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects (2000) - Wrapper Facade, Chapter 4 (Service Access and Configuration Patterns).
Schmidt, 'Wrapper Facade: A Structural Pattern for Encapsulating Functions within Classes', C++ Report 11(2), February 1999.
